newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia's Kalimantan still tense after riots.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia's Kalimantan still tense after riots.

text.p: Tension remained high in Indonesia's West Kalimantan province with troops on patrol following recent race riots between native Dayaks and Moslem migrants, residents and church sources said on Wednesday.
A curfew from 11 p.m. to 5 a.m. remained in place in Pontianak, the provincial port capital and rubber and trading centre on the west coast of Borneo island.
Residents in the town of Sanggau, 140 km (90 miles) east of Pontianak, said they were confined to their homes after 9 p.m.
They said there had been fighting around the remote riverside town last week between Dayaks and Moslem migrants from Madura island off Java's east coast.
"We are all afraid to be outside now. Troops are patrolling in the town because the situation is still tense," said one Sanggau resident contacted by telephone.
Police and military officials declined to comment on the situation on Wednesday.

Trouble broke out in West Kalimantan in late December, which police said was sparked by a fight between Dayak and Maduran youths over a girl at a concert in Sanggau Ledo, about 95 km (60 miles) north of Pontianak.
The military and local residents say at least 12 people have been killed over the past six weeks. Some residents and church sources say the figure could be much higher.
The Sanggau resident said Maduran families were still taking refuge in army camps in the area.
Residents said the Madurans were afraid to head to the coast by road because the Dayaks had set up roadblocks to examine passing vehicles.
Police in Sanggau said on Sunday the road to the coast had been reopened but residents reported only military traffic using it.
Madurans started voluntarily migrating to West Kalimantan in the late 1930s but those familiar with the area said the process had accelerated in the last 30 years.
A political analyst who visited the region earlier this month said the fighting, thought to be the fifth such outbreak in the last 20 years, was based on deep-seated racial hatred.
"Dayaks will only repeat over and over the ethnic stereotype that Madurese are knife-wielding, treacherous invaders who should be forced out of Kalimantan," the analyst told Reuters.

There are also large numbers of Moslem Javanese migrants who moved into the area as part of the government's resettlement programme to ease the population strain on overcrowded Java, but residents said they had not been the target of Dayak attacks.
They said West Kalimantan also had a large number of ethnic Chinese but these also had not been targeted, unlike in recent ethnic and religious rioting on Java.
In Pontianak, church sources said congregations were guarding their churches to prevent attacks by the Madurans.
The Dayaks are often Christian and the Madurans Moslem in mostly Islamic Indonesia, where at least 19 people have died since October in a number of religious and ethnic riots.
